subsection: 11. Case study: the Second Vatican Council

notes.h: Background: why the Council was called
notes.b: In the 1950s the Catholic Church was run from Rome and felt under pressure from the modern world. Pope John XXIII called a Council (a meeting of the bishops of the Church) to renew the Church and bring it into closer contact with that world.
points: In the 1950s the Church was led by the pope from Rome, the Mass was in Latin, power lay with a centralised Roman Curia (the Church's central administration), and priests and bishops were clearly separate from the laity (ordinary lay Catholics).

Pius XII (pope 1939–58) had centralised authority in Rome and ruled in an authoritarian style. This meant theologians demanding renewal had little voice, while by the 1950s the Church faced secularisation (the decline of religion in society), the loss of the working class in industrial Europe, communism and modern ideas.

The Reformation had split Christianity into Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, and the Catholic Church had long viewed the others with suspicion. The Church also faced the division between Catholics and other Christians, and the Holocaust and the long history of Christian anti-Judaism made Catholic–Jewish relations an urgent question.

Angelo Roncalli, patriarch of Venice, was elected Pope John XXIII on 28 October 1958, aged 76. He was seen as a caretaker pope, a short-term holder of the office, so his decision to call a Council surprised many.

He announced the Council on 25 January 1959 at the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls, to a group of cardinals, and this surprised them. It was the twenty-first ecumenical council (a Council of the whole Church) and the first since Vatican I (1869–70).

He used the Italian term aggiornamento, meaning bringing up to date, for its aim. He wanted a pastoral Council to renew the Church's teaching and practice rather than condemn errors, so that it could speak to ordinary people in a world of nuclear weapons, television and rapid change.

He also wanted Christian unity: the Council was meant to deal with the Church and the modern world, the liturgy (the Church's public worship) and relations with non-Catholic Christians. In 1960 he set up a Secretariat for Promoting Christian Unity under Cardinal Augustin Bea.

Preparatory commissions began work in 1960 and were dominated by Curia officials, including Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani, head of the Holy Office and of the theological commission. They expected a short Council that would simply approve prepared drafts, which set up the clash at the opening.
notes.tip: If asked why the Council was called, give John XXIII, aggiornamento, renewal and the modern world, and name the pressures on the Church. Don't confuse Vatican I (1869–70) with Vatican II (1962–65).

notes.b: The Council met in four autumn sessions in Rome. John XXIII opened it, but he died in June 1963 and Pope Paul VI carried it to its close, so be clear which pope did what.
points: The Council opened on 11 October 1962 in St Peter's Basilica, with about 2,500 bishops (the Council fathers) from all continents attending, along with observers from other Christian churches. About 2,500 is the figure for the opening only.

1. First session (autumn 1962): on 13 October the bishops, led by Cardinals Liénart of Lille and Frings of Cologne, asked for time before electing commission members, so the Curia's prepared drafts were not adopted. Reformers such as Frings, Suenens (Belgium) and Léger (Canada) gave it its own direction.

John XXIII died on 3 June 1963, and Cardinal Giovanni Battista Montini was elected Paul VI on 21 June 1963. Paul VI kept the Council going, which mattered because its future was in doubt after the death of the pope who had called it.

2. Second session (September to December 1963): the bishops debated the nature of the Church and collegiality, the idea that the bishops share authority with the pope. Sacrosanctum Concilium was promulgated (formally issued) on 4 December 1963.

3. Third session (September to 21 November 1964): Lumen Gentium and Unitatis Redintegratio were promulgated on 21 November 1964. The final tense week, when a conservative minority and last-minute papal changes caused conflict, was called Black Week.

4. Fourth session (September to 8 December 1965): Nostra Aetate (28 October), Dei Verbum (18 November), and Dignitatis Humanae and Gaudium et Spes (7 December) were promulgated. The Council closed on 8 December 1965, and Paul VI set up the Synod of Bishops in September 1965 to continue consultation.

Joseph Ratzinger, later Pope Benedict XVI, attended as a theological adviser, so the Council drew on expert theologians; and Karol Wojtyła (later John Paul II) took part as a bishop. Observers from Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches attended, and the press, radio and television covered the proceedings widely.
notes.tip: Dates of promulgation (1963, 1964, 1965) are not the same as session dates, and the documents were not all issued in 1965. Mixing up the popes is a common way to lose marks: John XXIII opened it and Paul VI completed it.

notes.b: The Council produced sixteen documents: four constitutions, nine decrees and three declarations. A constitution is the top rank of Council document, so the four constitutions set out its main teaching.
points: Sacrosanctum Concilium (1963), a constitution, reformed the liturgy. It allowed the use of local languages in the Mass so that people could take a fuller part in worship.

Lumen Gentium (1964), a constitution whose title means light of the nations, described the Church as the people of God. This gave a larger role to the laity and to the bishops collectively, which is the idea of collegiality.
Dei Verbum (1965), a constitution, addressed revelation (how God makes himself known) and Scripture, and it encouraged Catholics to study the Bible.
Gaudium et Spes (1965), a constitution whose title means joy and hope, addressed the Church in the modern world, including economic life, marriage, peace and social justice.
Unitatis Redintegratio (1964) was a decree, not a declaration. It committed the Church to ecumenism, the search for unity with other Christian churches.
Nostra Aetate (1965), a declaration, addressed non-Christian religions, including Judaism, and rejected the charge of collective Jewish guilt for the death of Christ.
Dignitatis Humanae (1965), a declaration, affirmed religious liberty, the right of people to follow their conscience in religion.
notes.tip: Marks usually go to the document's name plus its year plus what it said, so learn each with a one-line content. Don't confuse Nostra Aetate (non-Christian religions), Unitatis Redintegratio (other Christian churches) and Dignitatis Humanae (religious liberty).

notes.h: Changes in worship, relations and the Church
notes.b: The Council's decisions changed Catholic worship and the Church's relations with other faiths. These were its most visible results.
points: Local languages were used in parts of the Mass from 1964–65, and the new Roman Missal (Missal of Paul VI), issued in 1969 and in use 1969–70, completed the reform. The old Mass had been in Latin, so the vernacular Mass (in everyday language) made worship understandable.
The Council did not order the priest to face the people. The 1969–70 Missal made this common practice, so don't present it as a Council rule.
Lay Catholics were encouraged to take a more active part in worship, reading the Scriptures and serving as ministers. The laity's wider role also included parish councils.

The Church began dialogue with other Christian churches, and observers from those churches attended the sessions. This is the ecumenical movement, the movement among Christian churches to cooperate and move towards unity, which the Council endorsed in Unitatis Redintegratio.

On 7 December 1965 Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople lifted the mutual excommunications of 1054, which had marked the East–West split between the Catholic and Orthodox churches. They had met in Jerusalem in January 1964.

Nostra Aetate became the basis for improved Catholic–Jewish dialogue. John Paul II visited the Great Synagogue of Rome on 13 April 1986, widely described as the first papal visit to a synagogue, and called Jews the elder brothers of Christians.
Priests and religious orders were asked to return to their founders' ideals and to adapt their dress and rules, so many nuns changed their habits.

Dignitatis Humanae accepted the principle of religious liberty, that the state should not coerce people in matters of faith. This was a shift from the Church's earlier hostility to such liberty, though historians and theologians dispute how far it was a break rather than a development.
notes.tip: For the commonest paragraph on the changes, name the vernacular Mass with the new Missal, the lay role, ecumenism and relations with Judaism, with dates. Vernacular changes began in 1964–65 but the new Missal is 1969–70, and don't say the Council 'changed doctrine'.

notes.h: Reactions: traditionalists, progressives and Humanae Vitae
notes.b: The Council divided Catholics. Its reforms produced a traditionalist reaction, progressive demands for more change, and then a crisis over contraception.
points: Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, a French archbishop and a leading conservative at the Council, founded the Society of St Pius X in 1970. It rejected the Council's teaching on religious liberty and the new liturgy.
Lefebvre was excommunicated in 1988 after consecrating four bishops without papal approval. Keep the two dates apart: the Society dates from 1970 and the excommunication from 1988.
Progressive Catholics felt the reforms had stalled, because they argued the Council had not gone far enough on the role of women, on collegiality and on sexual ethics.

Humanae Vitae, issued by Paul VI on 25 July 1968, reaffirmed the ban on artificial contraception. It came after the Council closed and is Paul VI's teaching, not the Council's. It was widely rejected by Catholics in the West.

A papal commission on birth control reported in 1966 with a majority favouring a change after the introduction of the pill in the early 1960s. Paul VI did not follow it, so the ban's confirmation in 1968 came as a shock to many Catholics.
Theologians and bishops' conferences in the Netherlands, Belgium and West Germany voiced open dissent, and in practice many Catholic couples used contraception.
Humanae Vitae is seen as a turning point because it opened a gap between the Church's teaching and the practice of lay Catholics, and it weakened the authority of the clergy.

The Dutch Church, which held a pastoral council in 1968–70, was seen as the most progressive in Europe, and Rome moved to restore control under Paul VI and John Paul II. Many Western Catholics also attended Mass less often after the 1960s, a trend historians link to wider secularisation.
notes.tip: Explaining why Humanae Vitae divided Catholics earns credit for causes and consequences, so link it to the gap with lay practice. Don't present Humanae Vitae as a Council document.

notes.h: Key personality: Pope John Paul II (religious role)
notes.b: Karol Wojtyła, a Polish bishop who took part in the Council, was elected pope on 16 October 1978, the first non-Italian pope since 1523. He led the Church until his death on 2 April 2005, and his religious role shaped how the Council was interpreted.
points: Born in Wadowice, Poland, on 18 May 1920, Wojtyła became a priest, then auxiliary bishop of Kraków in 1958 and archbishop in 1964. He took part in the Second Vatican Council as a bishop and contributed to the drafting of Gaudium et Spes.

He made over a hundred foreign journeys (about 104), more than any previous pope, and drew huge crowds in Poland, Latin America, Africa and Europe. His first visit to Poland as pope, in June 1979, linked the Church with Polish national identity.

His 1979 visit and his support for Solidarity (founded in Poland in 1980) made him a political figure, so communist rulers saw him as a challenge. He met Gorbachev at the Vatican on 1 December 1989, a sign the Church had outlasted the communist regimes.

He visited Ireland from 29 September to 1 October 1979, the first papal visit to Ireland, saying Mass before about a million people in the Phoenix Park, Dublin. He also visited Drogheda, Galway, Knock and Limerick, and at Drogheda he appealed to paramilitaries to end violence.

He reaffirmed traditional teaching on contraception, abortion and the priesthood, and he opposed the ordination of women, liberation theology and a change to clerical celibacy. Under him the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, led by Cardinal Ratzinger from 1981, disciplined theologians.

He launched World Youth Days in the mid-1980s and promoted new movements such as Opus Dei and the Neocatechumenal Way. He also reached out beyond the Church, with the 1986 synagogue visit and a public act of repentance for the sins of Christians in the Jubilee year 2000.
He was shot in St Peter's Square on 13 May 1981 by Mehmet Ali Ağca and visited his attacker in prison in December 1983.

Contemporaries divided: supporters and crowds admired him, while critics saw a conservative turn after the Council. Historians disagree: supporters see a defender of human dignity and a world figure, while critics argue he resisted reform and handled abuse scandals badly.
notes.tip: Examiners often pair him with the Council or another figure, so give both his religious role (Council, travels, conservative teaching) and his role in Poland with similar weight. Giving only his political role loses marks, and a balanced judgement is rewarded.

notes.b: The Council's effect on practice is hard to judge because it coincided with wider social change such as secularisation, prosperity and the influence of the media. This makes the cause of decline disputed.
points: Attendance at Mass and vocations (calls to become a priest or member of a religious order) fell in Western Europe from the 1960s. Mass attendance fell steeply in the 1960s and 1970s, but Protestant churches declined too without any Council, which suggests social causes.
Vocations to the priesthood and religious life fell in the 1970s, as many priests and nuns left their orders in the years after the Council and fewer young people entered.
Attendance fell sharply in countries such as France and the Netherlands, while Poland and Ireland stayed relatively high. This difference shows that the effects of the Council varied by country.
In Ireland practice stayed high into the 1980s, but vocations and Mass attendance later began to fall, and the authority of the Church was shaken later still.

The Council did lead to increased lay involvement, in parish councils, readers and Eucharistic ministers (lay people who help give communion), and to a stronger Catholic interest in social justice and in peace.
notes.tip: Hedge the decline of practice: say the Council may have contributed but social change is also a cause, and note that Poland and Ireland were exceptions.

notes.h: Assessment: did the Council renew the Church?
notes.b: Historians differ on whether Vatican II was a successful renewal or a cause of decline. The judgement depends on which measure is used, so compare what the Council intended with what happened in practice.
points: Achievements: the vernacular liturgy, new relations with other faiths and churches, and a more open style of Church leadership.
Limits: falling practice, declining vocations to the priesthood, the conflict between traditionalists and progressives that continued after 1965, and the dispute over Humanae Vitae.
Contemporaries in the Church were divided: some saw the Council as a new beginning, while others saw it as a betrayal of tradition.
Later historians stress that the changes in religious practice were part of wider social trends, and that the Council's effects differed between countries.
Traditionalists blame the Council for the decline. Progressives argue instead that the Church failed to implement its reforms, especially on the role of women and collegiality.
notes.tip: A strong answer separates what the Council intended and enacted from what happened in practice, and uses both contemporaries and later historians.

keyTerms.definition: The movement among Christian churches to cooperate and reunite across denominational divisions, which the Council endorsed through Unitatis Redintegratio.
John XXIII's term for updating the Church's life and teaching to meet the modern world, the purpose behind the Council.
The celebration of the Mass in local languages rather than Latin, introduced by the Council's reform of worship.
The Council's 1965 declaration on non-Christian religions, which rejected collective Jewish guilt for the death of Christ.
Paul VI's 1968 encyclical reaffirming the Catholic ban on artificial contraception.
The right of individuals to follow their conscience in religious matters without coercion, affirmed by Dignitatis Humanae.
The principle affirmed at Vatican II that the bishops share responsibility for governing the Church with the pope.
The most authoritative kind of Council document; Vatican II issued four constitutions, on the liturgy, the Church, revelation and the Church in the modern world.
Ordinary church members who are not ordained, whose role in worship and Church life Vatican II enlarged.
